sections.heading: The AWS Well-Architected pillars
sections.body:
The framework has six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability. Treat them as a review checklist, not a one-time design gate. A good architecture makes trade-offs explicit, for example higher cost for lower latency or more durability for more complexity.

Use the Well-Architected review for a workload and act on the high-risk items before adding features.

sections.heading: Security and identity on AWS
sections.body:
Use AWS IAM for identity, with roles and temporary credentials for workloads instead of long-lived access keys. Prefer IAM Identity Center for human access. Enable MFA, least privilege, CloudTrail for audit, GuardDuty for threat detection and Security Hub for findings.

Encrypt data with KMS, keep keys rotation and ownership clear, use Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store for secrets, and segment networks with VPCs, subnets and security groups. Log everything that matters to an immutable, protected log account.

sections.heading: Compute and containers
sections.body:
EC2 for control, Auto Scaling groups for resilience, Elastic Beanstalk and App Runner for simpler apps, Lambda for event processing, ECS and EKS for containers, Fargate for serverless containers.

Choose by team capability and operational burden. A managed service that the team cannot debug is not an advantage. Use Spot instances for fault-tolerant batch work and Savings Plans or Reserved Instances for steady state after a baseline.

sections.heading: Storage, databases and caching
sections.body:
S3 for object storage with lifecycle rules and versioning. EBS for block storage. EFS for shared file systems. Glacier for cold archive.

Databases: RDS or Aurora for relational, DynamoDB for key-value with predictable access, ElastiCache for caching, Redshift for analytics. Choose based on access patterns, not familiarity. Add ElastiCache or DynamoDB Accelerator where latency demands it, and design backups and point-in-time recovery explicitly.

sections.heading: Networking and edge
sections.body:
Design VPCs with public and private subnets across multiple availability zones. Use Application Load Balancer or Network Load Balancer for ingress, Transit Gateway for hub connectivity, Route 53 for DNS, CloudFront for content delivery and AWS Global Accelerator for global traffic. Connect hybrid networks with VPN or Direct Connect.

Keep data paths private where possible using VPC endpoints and PrivateLink. Design egress costs deliberately; they dominate many bills.

sections.heading: Event driven, integration and reliability
sections.body:
Use SNS, SQS, EventBridge and Step Functions to decouple components. Prefer asynchronous, event-driven designs for resilience and scalability. Design for failure: health checks, retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, timeouts and circuit breakers.

Reliability also means tested backups, multi-AZ deployments, cross-region strategies where warranted, capacity planning, and documented failover. A system that fails fast and recovers is better than one that hides faults.

sections.heading: Cost optimisation
sections.body: Tag every resource, allocate costs and review monthly. Right-size, delete unused resources, use lifecycle rules for storage and inexpensive storage classes. Use Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets with alerts. Commit to Savings Plans only after a usage baseline, and prefer Savings Plans over Reserved Instances for flexibility. Serverless is not automatically cheaper; model the workload.

sections.heading: Decision method for AWS solutions architect work
sections.body:
A defensible AWS design states the workload, the failure modes to survive, the access patterns, the security boundary, the recovery target and the cost. Then it chooses the smallest managed service that meets those constraints, and documents what would change the choice.

The trap is choosing services for familiarity. The CTO-style answer is a decision record with trade-offs and an exit price.

workedExample.title: AWS architecture for Cretek reporting pipeline (illustrative)
workedExample.body: Requirement: ingest nightly school data exports, transform and report, retain seven years for audit, recover within 24 hours. Design: S3 for raw landing zone with versioning and lifecycle to Glacier. AWS Glue or Lambda for transform. DynamoDB or RDS for reporting aggregates depending on query patterns. EventBridge to trigger jobs. CloudWatch alarms on failures. IAM role for the pipeline with least privilege. S3 bucket policy protecting raw data. Cost driven by storage duration and Glacier retrieval times.

misconceptions: Designing a single availability zone for production.
Storing long-lived access keys on instances.
Ignoring egress and cross-region data transfer.
Adding Aurora when the workload is simple key-value.
Treating backups as a substitute for tested recovery.
learn.explainTask: In 150 words or fewer, explain to a chief executive why an AWS design should start from failure modes and cost, rather than from the most popular services.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which AWS service provides tamper-evident audit logs of API calls?
knowledgeCheck.why: CloudTrail records AWS API calls for audit and governance.

knowledgeCheck.question: For a key-value workload with predictable access at low latency, which database is usually preferred?
knowledgeCheck.why: DynamoDB is optimised for key-value and predictable low-latency access.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which compute option removes server management for containerised workloads?
knowledgeCheck.why: Fargate runs containers without managing EC2 instances.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of a dead-letter queue?
options: Hold messages that could not be processed
knowledgeCheck.why: A dead-letter queue captures messages that exceed retry limits for later inspection.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which AWS feature delivers content with low latency globally?
knowledgeCheck.why: CloudFront is a content delivery network.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which practice best reduces long-term compute cost for a steady-state workload?
options: Use Savings Plans after a baseline
knowledgeCheck.why: Savings Plans reward steady commit after measuring usage. Spot is for fault-tolerant work, not steady baseload.

build.business: Cretek uses AWS for reporting and audit data. Costs, recovery and security must be defensible to schools and regulators.
build.problem: Design and document a defensible AWS architecture for one reporting or audit workload, including security, network, data, async processing, recovery, observability and cost.
requirements: State the workload, data volumes, retention and recovery target
Define the security boundary: accounts, IAM roles, KMS, logging and network isolation
Choose AWS services for compute, storage, database and integration with a reason for each
Design an event-driven or batch processing flow with failure handling and dead-letter queues
Define backups and tested recovery steps
Estimate monthly cost with a cited price list and date
Define observability with metrics, logs, traces and alarms with owners
Write a Well-Architected style risk list and mitigations
Every figure labelled REAL, ASSUMPTION or SIMULATED
constraints: No long-lived access keys in code or images
No production data in test environments
Cost estimates must use current AWS pricing
Infrastructure must be reproducible and documented
build.design: Write a one-page design listing failure modes, service choices, security boundary, recovery target, cost and the alternative you rejected.
tasks: Draft the security and account structure
Design the network and data flow
acceptance: Recovery is designed and tested or scheduled
Cost estimate is dated and labelled
Well-Architected risks are listed with mitigations
No long-lived credentials in the repository
build.deliverable: AWS architecture decision record, infrastructure-as-code, Well-Architected risk list, cost estimate and recovery runbook, referenced by path.

defend.scenario: The chief executive wants to know if the AWS setup is secure, what a failure costs and whether it can be cheaper.
prompts: How is patient or school data protected on AWS?
What happens if one availability zone fails?
Why these services instead of simpler or cheaper ones?
What drives the monthly bill and how could it fall?

rubric.criterion: Security boundary and auditability are explicit
Reliability design matches the recovery target
Open risks are honest and prioritised
